title: The Client Named a Tool. That's Not the Same as a Diagnosis.
description: When a client asks for 'an AI chatbot,' the actual bottleneck is often somewhere the chatbot would never touch — and building it anyway looks like progress while fixing almost nothing.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a client's requested tool from the actual process bottleneck it may not address
Identify when integration/consolidation work needs to precede an AI feature, not follow it

contentSections.body: A client says, 'We want an AI chatbot for customer support.' You look at their actual process: tickets arrive by email, through a web contact form, and in a shared Slack channel customers have started using informally — three separate queues, no unified view, and support staff manually copy-paste between them before anyone even reads a ticket. Building an AI chatbot that answers questions in one of those three channels would look like progress and fix almost nothing: two-thirds of tickets still arrive somewhere the chatbot never sees, and the actual daily pain — manually consolidating three inboxes — is untouched.

This is the core consulting-specific skill in tool selection: the client named a tool before anyone diagnosed the actual bottleneck, and the two aren't always the same. A capable tool-selection process starts with the workflow, not the tool catalog — where does work actually get stuck, lost, or duplicated?

In this case, the higher-leverage first deliverable is often boring integration work — a shared inbox, ticket-routing rules, or a lightweight automation to consolidate the three channels into one queue — that has to exist before an AI response tool has a single place to operate on. Skipping straight to the AI feature the client asked for, without that groundwork, means layering intelligence onto only a third of the actual workload.

contentSections.code:
Client's process: tickets arrive via email, a web form, and an informal Slack channel — three separate queues, manually cross-checked by staff.
Proposed deliverable: an AI chatbot answering questions in the web form's chat widget only.
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in recommending the AI chatbot as the first deliverable here?

options.label: It only addresses one of three fragmented intake channels, leaving the actual bottleneck — consolidation — unsolved
AI chatbots are never a useful tool for customer support
AI chatbots are too expensive for a client this size

feedback.addresses-one-of-three-channels: Correct. The client's actual daily pain is fragmentation across three unconnected queues, and a chatbot embedded in only one of them doesn't touch the other two-thirds of ticket volume or the manual cross-checking that's the real time sink. It looks like an AI deliverable was shipped, while the process problem the client actually has remains exactly as broken.
feedback.chatbots-never-useful: The lesson isn't that chatbots are never useful — a well-scoped one can be a strong deliverable once there's a single consolidated queue for it to operate on. The flaw is sequencing: recommending it before the fragmentation problem is solved.
feedback.too-expensive: Cost isn't the issue being raised here — the issue is that the recommended tool doesn't address where the client's actual bottleneck lives, regardless of price.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The chatbot proposal looks like progress because it's a real, deployable AI feature — but scoping it to "the web form" instead of "the actual fragmented intake process" means it only ever sees a third of the workload. Diagnosing the real bottleneck (three disconnected queues) before recommending any tool would have surfaced that consolidation, not a chatbot, is the higher-leverage first deliverable.

contentSections.scenario:
You're about to tell this client that their first deliverable should be ticket consolidation, not the chatbot they asked for. That's an unwelcome answer, so the findings you cite have to do real work.

Some of what you know about their process supports the recommendation. Some of it is true but supports nothing, and citing it weakens the case.
contentSections.question: Select every finding that genuinely supports recommending consolidation before the chatbot.

items.label: Tickets arrive through three separate queues with no unified view
Staff manually copy between queues before anyone has read a ticket
A chatbot in the web form's widget would never see the email or Slack tickets
Routing rules are a more established technology than chatbots
The Slack channel is informal, so its tickets can be left out of scope
The client named the chatbot themselves, without a diagnosis

explanation.three-queues: Applicable. This is the diagnosis. Three unconnected intake points with no single view is the structural fact everything else follows from, and it's checkable — the client can look at it and agree.
explanation.manual-copy: Applicable. This is where the daily cost actually lands. It names time being spent on work that would disappear if intake were consolidated, which is what makes consolidation a deliverable rather than tidying.
explanation.widget-blind: Applicable, and it's the sequencing argument. It doesn't say the chatbot is wrong — it says the chatbot has no complete queue to work on yet, which is a reason to do one before the other rather than instead of it.
explanation.chatbot-modern: Not applicable. How established a technology is has nothing to do with which one addresses this client's bottleneck, and leading with it invites an argument about technology preferences instead of about their process.
explanation.slack-informal: Not applicable, and it works against you. Declaring a channel out of scope doesn't move the tickets somewhere else — customers keep using it and staff keep handling them. Scoping around inconvenient volume is how a deliverable ends up covering less of the real workload than the slide suggests.
explanation.client-named-it: Not applicable as evidence. It's true, and it explains how the request arrived, but it's an observation about the client rather than a finding about their process. Cited out loud it reads as "you asked for the wrong thing," which is the fastest way to lose the room.

contentSections.synthesis: The three findings that work are all statements about the client's own process that they can verify. The three that don't are about technology preference, scope convenience, or the client's reasoning — none of which survive a challenge, and one of which makes the conversation adversarial. When you're delivering a recommendation someone didn't ask for, the evidence has to be things they can check themselves.

contentSections.question: A client opens with "we want an AI chatbot for customer support." Put these steps in the order that reaches a real diagnosis before a tool is chosen.
steps: List every channel a ticket can arrive through
Trace one real ticket from arrival to resolution, noting each manual handoff
Name where work gets stuck, lost, or re-entered by hand
Decide whether the bottleneck is in intake, routing, or answering
Choose a tool that acts on the bottleneck you named
Tell the client which parts of their original request this does and does not cover
contentSections.explanation: Listing the channels comes first because it's what reveals the three queues — a request for "a chatbot for support" doesn't. Tracing a real ticket end to end is what turns that list into a picture of where time goes; asking people to describe the process in general tends to produce the tidy version. Only then can you name the stuck points, and only then does the intake-versus-routing-versus-answering question have an answer. Tool choice is the second-to-last step, not the first. The final step is the one that gets skipped under pressure, and it's what stops the gap between what was asked for and what was delivered from being discovered three months in.

contentSections.body: Tool selection starts with diagnosing where the process actually breaks, not with the tool the client named first. Sometimes the right first recommendation is boring integration work, not the AI feature they asked for — and naming that clearly, even when it's not what was requested, is the actual consulting skill.

title: RAG or Fine-Tuning: the Question Nobody Asks First
description: Choosing between retrieval-augmented generation and a fine-tuned model isn't about which is more advanced — it's about whether the client needs answers that cite and update against live source documents.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific requirement that makes RAG the right architecture over a fine-tuned model
Recognize when a client's stated preference for one architecture doesn't match their actual requirement

contentSections.body: A client's internal HR team wants an AI assistant that answers employee questions about company policy — benefits, leave, expense rules. They've heard fine-tuning is "more advanced" and ask you to fine-tune a model on their policy documents. Meanwhile, their legal team updates the leave policy twice a year, and HR has been burned before by an intranet search tool that kept surfacing a policy PDF that was two revisions out of date. Fine-tuning is the wrong call here, and it has nothing to do with the technology being less capable.

This is a genuinely common tool-selection trap: a client names an architecture because it sounds more sophisticated, without the requirement actually pointing there. The real diagnostic question for RAG versus fine-tuning isn't "which is better" — it's:

**Does the answer need to cite a specific, current source document, and does that source change over time?**

If yes, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the right architecture: the model retrieves the current version of a document at answer time and grounds its response in it, so when the leave policy changes, updating the answer means updating the document — not retraining anything. A fine-tuned model, by contrast, bakes knowledge into its weights at training time; when the source policy changes, the model's "knowledge" is now silently stale until someone notices and retrains it — a much slower, more expensive, and easier-to-miss failure mode than a RAG system citing an outdated doc (which at least surfaces a checkable citation).

contentSections.scenario:
Two internal AI tool requests:

A) HR policy assistant — answers must reflect the current leave/benefits policy, which legal updates twice a year, and HR wants employees able to see which policy document an answer came from.

B) A tool that generates a consistent, on-brand tone summary of quarterly sales trends across regions, from stable historical data that doesn't change after each quarter closes.
contentSections.question: Which scenario is the stronger case for RAG over a fine-tuned model, and why?

options.label: Scenario A — the source document changes over time and answers need to cite it
Scenario B — summarizing sales trends needs the most current-sounding language
Both are equally strong cases for RAG, since either could technically use it

feedback.scenario-a-rag: Correct. Scenario A has exactly the two conditions that make RAG the right call: the underlying policy document changes on a real schedule, and answers need to be traceable to a specific, checkable source. Scenario B's data is stable once a quarter closes and doesn't require citation — a fine-tuned model (or even a much simpler templated summary) fits it fine, without RAG's added retrieval-pipeline complexity.
feedback.scenario-b-rag: Sales-trend summarization doesn't need live retrieval against a changing source — the data is fixed once the quarter closes, and the deliverable is a consistent tone/style, which is closer to what fine-tuning (or simpler prompting) is suited for. Adding a retrieval pipeline here is unnecessary complexity for a requirement that isn't there.
feedback.both-equal: The two scenarios differ on exactly the diagnostic question that matters — whether the source changes and needs citation. Treating them as equally strong RAG cases means the diagnostic isn't actually being applied; it's the difference between the two that determines the right architecture.

contentSections.concept: RAG earns its complexity specifically when answers must be grounded in and traceable to a source that changes over time. When the underlying data is stable and citation isn't required, the added retrieval-pipeline machinery is cost without a matching benefit — the diagnostic question, not which architecture sounds more advanced, is what should drive the recommendation.

contentSections.scenario:
Back to the HR policy assistant. The client asked for fine-tuning; you're going to recommend RAG instead, and you need the requirement to carry the argument rather than your preference.

Some of what you know about this client points at RAG specifically. Some of it is true of the project but would be equally true if fine-tuning were the right call.
contentSections.question: Select every requirement that genuinely points to RAG rather than a fine-tuned model.

items.label: Legal revises the leave policy twice a year
HR wants employees to see which policy document an answer came from
The team has already been burned by a tool surfacing a policy two revisions out of date
The client wants an architecture that will read as sophisticated to their board
Answers should sound consistent and on-brand
Employees ask questions in casual, varied wording

explanation.source-changes: Applicable, and it's the core of the argument. A source on a revision schedule is exactly the condition where baking knowledge into weights goes stale between retrainings, and where updating a document is the whole update path.
explanation.citation-needed: Applicable. Traceability to a specific document is something retrieval gives you structurally — the answer was built from a retrieved passage, so the passage can be shown. A fine-tuned model can be asked to name a source, but it has no retrieved document to point at.
explanation.stale-history: Applicable. It's the requirement stated as a scar rather than a spec, which is often how the real requirement arrives. It tells you staleness is the failure mode this team will actually judge the system by.
explanation.sounds-advanced: Not applicable — this is the reason the client asked for fine-tuning in the first place, and it points at whichever architecture currently sounds most impressive rather than at anything about the work. Building the recommendation on it means rebuilding when the fashion moves.
explanation.consistent-tone: Not applicable — and if anything it's the one requirement here that leans the other way. Reproducing a consistent style is closer to what fine-tuning suits. It isn't a strong enough requirement on its own to outweigh the changing source, but it isn't evidence for RAG.
explanation.varied-wording: Not applicable. Handling casual, varied phrasing is something a capable model does either way. It's a requirement about the model, not about the architecture wrapped around it, so it can't decide between the two.

contentSections.synthesis: The three requirements that decide this are all about the source document: it changes, it has to be citable, and going stale is the failure this team has already lived through. The three that don't decide it are about how the system sounds or how the choice will be perceived. When the client has named an architecture, going back to the requirement is what turns the conversation from a disagreement about technology into a check against something they can confirm about their own work.

contentSections.intro: Write the recommendation the way it will go to the client — as a small set of decisions, each with a reason, rather than a single architecture name. Four fields.

fields.prompt: Which architecture goes in the recommendation?

options.label: retrieval-augmented generation
fine-tuned model

feedback.retrieval-augmented generation: Right — the source changes on a schedule and answers need to be traceable to it, which is the pair of conditions RAG exists for.
feedback.fine-tuned model: This is what the client asked for, but the requirement doesn't support it here. A fine-tuned model's knowledge is fixed at training time, so every policy revision leaves it confidently out of date until someone notices and retrains.

fields.prompt: What does an answer get grounded in at the moment it's produced?

options.label: the current policy document, retrieved at answer time
options.value: the current policy document, retrieved at answer time

options.label: the knowledge held in the model's weights
options.value: the knowledge held in the model's weights

fields.correctValue: the current policy document, retrieved at answer time

feedback.the current policy document, retrieved a: Right — retrieving at answer time is what makes the answer reflect the version that exists now rather than the version that existed at training.
feedback.the knowledge held in the model's weight: This is the fine-tuning answer, and it's the mechanism behind the staleness problem. Weights hold whatever was true when training ran, and nothing in the system flags when that stops matching the live policy.

fields.prompt: What has to happen when legal revises the leave policy?

options.label: publish the revised document to the store the assistant reads
options.value: publish the revised document to the store the assistant reads

options.label: schedule a retraining run on the new policy set
options.value: schedule a retraining run on the new policy set

fields.correctValue: publish the revised document to the store the assistant reads

feedback.publish the revised document to the stor: Right — and this is the field the client will care about most. The update path is a step legal already takes, not a technical project scheduled after the fact.
feedback.schedule a retraining run on the new pol: This is what the client would be signing up for with fine-tuning: every policy revision becomes a retraining project, and the window between the revision and the retrain is time the assistant is confidently wrong.

fields.prompt: What ships alongside each answer, so HR can check it?

options.label: a link to the source policy document and its version
options.value: a link to the source policy document and its version

options.label: a confidence score for the answer
options.value: a confidence score for the answer

fields.correctValue: a link to the source policy document and its version

feedback.a link to the source policy document and: Right — this is the requirement HR actually stated, and the version matters as much as the link given what happened with the out-of-date PDF.
feedback.a confidence score for the answer: A score tells an employee how sure the system is, which isn't what HR asked for and isn't checkable. A high-confidence answer drawn from a superseded policy looks exactly like a high-confidence answer drawn from the current one.

contentSections.synthesis: Read as a whole, the recommendation makes the argument without needing the word RAG in it: answers are grounded in the current document, updates happen by publishing, and every answer carries a checkable source. That's what the client can evaluate. The architecture name is the consequence of those four decisions, not the thing being sold — which also means that if the requirements changed, the recommendation would visibly change with them rather than needing to be re-argued.

contentSections.body: A client asking for "fine-tuning" or "RAG" by name is naming a solution, not a requirement — same trap as a client naming a tool in the previous lesson. Ask whether the real need is a changing, citable source document (RAG) or a stable pattern/style to reproduce (fine-tuning or simpler prompting), and let that answer drive the recommendation instead of what sounds more technically impressive.

title: The categories: models, orchestration, RPA, and the existing software
description: A vendor pitch for 'an AI platform' is usually one of four different kinds of tool wearing the same marketing language — knowing which one actually solves a stated need stops you buying the wrong layer.

learningObjectives.text: Sort a stated automation need into the category of tool that actually addresses it — existing software, orchestration, RPA, or a model
Recognize when an already-licensed system solves the need without any new tool

contentSections.body: Halsted Underwriting writes specialty marine cargo cover for about forty accounts a week. After a vendor demo, the operations director tells you, "we need an AI platform for claims intake." What she means, concretely, is narrower: claim number, policy number, and claimed amount currently get typed by hand out of PDFs that brokers email in, into the claims system Halsted bought eighteen months ago. Nobody has yet asked what that claims system can already do on its own.

"We need an AI platform" collapses four genuinely different kinds of tool into one phrase, and picking the wrong one is an expensive way to find out they're different.

**The software you already have.** Most claims, CRM, or ERP platforms bought in the last several years ship with some rules engine, email-ingestion feature, or field-mapping capability that's simply never been turned on — often because activating it wasn't clearly anyone's job. This is always worth checking first: it's already paid for, already integrated, and carries no new vendor risk.

**Orchestration platforms.** Tools (no-code platforms, or bespoke pipeline code) that connect a model to your other systems and sequence the steps between them. They don't add intelligence — they route it. Buying one gets you a conveyor belt, not a capability to put on it.

**RPA (robotic process automation).** Drives an existing system's own screen the way a person would — clicking, typing, reading fields — for systems that have no API to talk to directly. Genuinely useful where an API doesn't exist and isn't coming. Fragile: it breaks whenever the target screen's layout changes.

**A foundation model or API.** Raw language- or vision-understanding capability. Needs to be wired up and prompted by something else; it doesn't arrive as a finished workflow.

The order to check them in isn't "which is newest" — it's existing software, then orchestration or RPA to connect what already exists, and a model only for the specific piece that's genuinely a language- or vision-understanding problem none of the above can do.

contentSections.scenario: Halsted's claims system — the one bought eighteen months ago — turns out, once someone actually reads its admin documentation, to already have a built-in email-ingestion module with configurable field mapping. Nobody enabled it because IT assumed it required a paid add-on it doesn't.
contentSections.question: Before evaluating any new tool for the claim-intake problem, which category should be checked first?

options.label: The existing claims system's own unused capability
A foundation model API that reads the PDFs and extracts the fields
An RPA bot that opens each email and re-types the fields into the claims system

feedback.existing-software: Right. A capability that's already licensed, already integrated, and just switched off is the cheapest possible fix and carries no new vendor risk — and even if it turns out not to be sufficient on its own, you now know exactly what gap a new tool actually needs to close, instead of guessing.
feedback.model-api: This might still be part of the eventual answer, but reaching for it first skips a much cheaper fix that may already exist. The category question comes before the vendor question.
feedback.rpa: RPA solves a different problem — stitching together a system that has no API. Halsted's claims system does have an admin interface with a real ingestion feature; the fix here is turning it on, not building a robot to fake using it by hand.

contentSections.concept: Checking the existing software first isn't caution for its own sake — it's the cheapest hypothesis to rule out, and ruling it out first tells you exactly what a new tool would actually need to add.

contentSections.title: What each category actually can't do

contentSections.body:
Each category also has a real limit worth naming to a client before they buy it, because a vendor pitch rarely volunteers its own category's weak point.

The existing software's built-in rules can map a field to a field, but they can't judge an ambiguous document or read free text the way a broker's cover-note attachment is written — that's still a model's job. An orchestration platform doesn't get more intelligent the more it costs; it only routes whatever intelligence you plug into it, so a client sold an expensive orchestration tool with no model behind it has bought a conveyor belt with nothing on it. RPA is fragile in a specific, recurring way: it breaks the moment the target system's screen layout changes, which is a real ongoing maintenance cost that almost never appears in the initial quote. And a model API by itself has no memory or sequencing — every call is stateless unless something else (an orchestration layer) holds state and calls it in order.

contentSections.scenario: A vendor pitches Halsted "an AI claims platform" that bundles a document-reading model, a drag-and-drop workflow builder, and automatic broker-notification emails, all under one subscription. You're deciding what in the pitch is a genuinely new capability for Halsted and what's marketing language wrapped around something Halsted effectively already has.
contentSections.question: Select every part of the pitch that represents a genuine new capability Halsted doesn't already have.

items.label: It reads the broker's PDF claim form and extracts the claimed amount and policy number from free-text layouts
It includes a drag-and-drop workflow builder for sequencing the intake steps
It automatically emails the broker to confirm receipt of the claim
It maps extracted fields into named fields in a claims record
It can extract fields from a scanned, slightly crooked photo of a paper claim form, not just a clean PDF
It has a polished dashboard showing claims processed this week

explanation.reads-pdf: Applicable. Reading free-text layouts and judging which number is the claimed amount is exactly the language-understanding task none of Halsted's existing pieces can do — this is the genuine new capability, and the actual reason to consider a model at all.
explanation.workflow-builder: Not applicable as a new capability — Halsted's claims system already sequences intake steps once fields are populated. Paying for a second workflow builder duplicates that, it doesn't add anything.
explanation.broker-email: Not applicable. Confirmation emails are already something Halsted's existing email and claims tools can trigger; wrapping it in the new platform's branding doesn't make it a new capability.
explanation.field-mapping-dup: Not applicable, for the same reason as the existing software's own field-mapping module in the earlier scenario — mapping an extracted value into a named field is exactly what the already-licensed claims system does once given the value.
explanation.handles-scans: Applicable. A crooked scanned photo is a harder version of the same document-understanding problem the clean PDF case needs — genuinely something the existing rules-based mapping can't do on its own.
explanation.dashboard: Not applicable. A dashboard is a reporting view over data Halsted's claims system already holds once a claim is logged — it doesn't change what gets automated, only how it's displayed.

contentSections.synthesis: The two items that hold up are both instances of the same thing: reading and judging free-form input, which is the one job in this pitch that genuinely needs a model. Everything else in the bundle is a feature Halsted's existing claims system already performs, repackaged under the new platform's name. The useful move with any "AI platform" pitch is separating what's actually new from what's just been re-skinned.

contentSections.body: Category before vendor name. Check the existing software first, use orchestration or RPA to connect what already exists, and reach for a model only for the piece that's genuinely a language- or vision-understanding problem.

title: Buy, wire together, or build: choosing honestly
description: Deciding whether a need should be bought off the shelf, wired from existing pieces, or custom-built — using maintenance ownership, format variability, and cost shape as the criteria, not which option is more interesting to build.

learningObjectives.text: Choose between buying, wiring together, and building a solution using maintenance, variability, and cost-shape criteria
Recognize when 'build' is being chosen for the wrong reason rather than genuine fit

contentSections.body: Halsted's operations analyst, who's handy with Python, offers to "just build our own extraction script" for the claim PDFs over a long weekend, at no cost beyond his time. It works, on the current broker PDF template. Six months later one broker changes their claim-form layout, and the script quietly starts extracting the wrong field into "claimed amount" for that broker's claims. Nobody notices for three weeks, because a weekend project has no monitoring the way a maintained vendor tool would.

Buy, wire together, or build isn't a preference — it's a decision with three honest criteria.

**Who maintains it after it ships, and on what schedule.** A bought tool's maintenance is the vendor's job, priced into the subscription. A built tool's maintenance is whoever wrote it, for as long as they're at the company and paying attention — which, as Halsted found out, can be nobody, silently, the moment a broker changes a form layout.

**How much the input actually varies.** A narrow, stable input (one broker, one template, rarely changing) is a reasonable build. A wide, drifting one (dozens of brokers, each with their own layout, changing without notice) is exactly the case a maintained vendor tool is priced to absorb, because the vendor is spreading that maintenance cost across many customers.

**The shape of the cost, not just the size.** Buying costs money continuously and predictably. Building costs one person's time now, and then again every time something breaks — a cost that's real but invisible until it lands, and lands on whoever's available that week, not on a maintenance budget line.

The honest fourth question, and the one people skip: is "build" being chosen because it genuinely fits better on those three criteria, or because it's more interesting to build than to configure a vendor tool? Both are real motivations. Only one belongs in the recommendation.

contentSections.code:
Analyst's weekend-build plan, as pitched to the ops director:

"I'll write a Python script that opens each claim PDF, pulls out the claim number, policy number, and claimed amount using regex patterns matched to our current broker templates, and writes them into the claims system's import CSV. Should take a weekend. Free, and I already know the codebase."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this plan that the pitch doesn't mention at all?

options.label: There's no plan for what happens when a broker's template changes and the regex patterns stop matching correctly
Python is the wrong programming language for this kind of task
A weekend is too long to spend on a script this small

feedback.no-drift-plan: Correct. The plan is scoped entirely to Halsted's current templates, with nothing said about what happens when one changes — no monitoring to notice a drop in extraction accuracy, no owner assigned to update the patterns, no schedule for re-checking. That gap is exactly what let the wrong-field extraction run silently for three weeks.
feedback.wrong-language: Language choice isn't the issue — regex-based extraction in Python is a perfectly reasonable approach for a stable, narrow input. The flaw is about what happens when the input stops being stable, not about the tool used to handle it.
feedback.too-long: Time spent isn't the flaw either — a weekend is actually cheap relative to a vendor subscription. The problem is what isn't in the plan for after the weekend, not how long the weekend itself takes.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A build proposal that names what it does but not who maintains it, and on what trigger, is missing the part that determines whether "free" stays free. The three-week silent failure wasn't a bug in the regex — it was the predictable result of a plan with no owner and no drift detection, which is a maintenance decision, not a coding one.

contentSections.intro: Write the buy/wire/build recommendation for Halsted's claim-extraction need the way it should go in a proposal — as explicit decisions, not a single word. Three fields.

fields.prompt: Given roughly a dozen different broker PDF templates that change without notice, which path fits best?

options.label: buy a maintained extraction tool
build an in-house script

feedback.buy: Right. A dozen templates changing without notice is exactly the wide, drifting input case a vendor is priced to absorb — they're maintaining pattern coverage across many customers' template changes, which is a cost Halsted would otherwise carry alone, on a weekend, reactively.
feedback.build: This is what the analyst offered, and it fit the plan's stated scope (current templates) but not the actual input variability — a dozen templates that change without notice is precisely the case a single maintainer, doing this alongside their real job, tends to fall behind on.

fields.prompt: Whichever path is chosen, who is explicitly responsible for noticing when extraction accuracy drops?

options.label: a named owner with it in their actual job description, checked on a schedule
whoever happens to notice a claim looks wrong

feedback.named-owner: Right. "Whoever notices" is exactly the plan that produced three silent weeks — an unassigned responsibility is the same as no responsibility until something visibly breaks.
feedback.whoever-notices: This is the actual failure mode from the hook, restated as a plan. It relies on a wrong extraction being visibly wrong, which the whole earlier module on silent failure showed you can't count on.

fields.prompt: How should the ops director think about the cost difference between the two paths?

options.label: buy is a predictable recurring cost; build is a smaller upfront cost plus an unscheduled, unbudgeted cost every time something breaks
build is simply cheaper, since it's free

feedback.shape: Right. "Free" only describes the weekend. The real cost of the build path is the analyst's time every time a template changes, landing unpredictably on whichever week that happens, which is a genuinely different shape of cost than a subscription line even if the totals turned out similar.
feedback.free: This is the trap in the analyst's own pitch — it counts the weekend and stops there. The three weeks of wrong extractions were also a cost, just one that didn't show up on an invoice.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these three answers are about which option is "better" in the abstract — they're about matching the path to Halsted's actual input variability, naming a real owner instead of hoping someone notices, and being honest that build's low upfront cost isn't the same as low total cost. That's the recommendation a client can actually evaluate.

contentSections.body: Buy, wire together, or build is a decision made on maintenance ownership, input variability, and cost shape — not on which option is free this weekend or more interesting to write.

title: Total cost including the parts nobody quotes
description: A vendor's sticker price leaves out the review labor, the exception handling, the volume-scaling, and the re-testing a tool needs when its inputs drift — and those are usually most of what the tool actually costs.

learningObjectives.text: Name the recurring cost categories a vendor quote typically omits
Build a total-cost picture for a proposed tool that goes beyond its subscription price

contentSections.body: A vendor quotes Halsted $600 a month for a claims-extraction API. The operations director's first reaction: "that's basically free compared to hiring someone." It isn't, once you count what she didn't ask about: someone still has to review every extraction before it posts to the claims system, currently budgeted at zero hours because nobody scoped that step; the pricing is usage-based and claim volume is projected to roughly double next year; and someone at Halsted has to own re-testing the tool every time the broker community's form templates shift, which — per the tool-selection categories lesson — they do, without notice.

A quote's sticker price is the easiest number to compare and the least complete one. The categories that usually don't make it into a vendor's pitch deck: **review labor** — almost no extraction tool is trusted to post unchecked, so someone's time reviewing outputs is a real, recurring cost that scales with volume the same way the subscription does; **exception handling** — the share of inputs the tool can't confidently process at all, which still has to go somewhere, usually a person, and that share is rarely in the marketing accuracy number; **volume-scaling pricing** — a quote based on today's volume can look very different once usage-based pricing meets next year's growth; and **maintenance and re-testing** — the recurring cost, in someone's time, of confirming the tool still performs when the inputs it depends on inevitably drift.

contentSections.scenario: The vendor's marketing figure for the extraction API is "95% field accuracy," measured on their own benchmark set. Before you see Halsted's actual result, make a guess.
contentSections.question: On Halsted's real, varied broker PDF submissions — a dozen different templates, several of them scanned rather than digitally generated — what percentage of claims will actually need a human to correct at least one extracted field?
contentSections.explanation: Once Halsted tested the tool on its own claim mix, 24% of claims needed at least one field corrected by a person — nowhere near the 95% headline figure suggests. The gap isn't the vendor lying; it's the same mechanism from the capability-numbers lesson in the previous phase: a benchmark accuracy figure is measured on the vendor's chosen test set, and Halsted's actual mix of scanned, non-standard broker templates is harder than that set. The 95% number answers "how does this perform in general"; the 24% answers the only question that matters for budgeting review labor at Halsted specifically.

contentSections.scenario: You're building the total-cost picture to put next to the vendor's $600/month quote before Halsted signs. Some of what you know belongs in that picture. Some of it is true but doesn't change the cost comparison.
contentSections.question: Select every fact that genuinely belongs in the total-cost picture.

items.label: Every extraction currently has to be reviewed by a person before it posts, and nobody has budgeted hours for that
The pricing is usage-based, and claim volume is projected to roughly double next year
24% of claims need at least one field corrected on Halsted's actual document mix
The vendor was founded two years ago
The vendor's live demo, on the vendor's own sample documents, looked impressively fast
Someone at Halsted needs to own re-testing the tool whenever broker templates shift, and that isn't scoped as anyone's job yet

explanation.review-hours: Applicable. Review labor is a real, recurring cost the $600 quote says nothing about, and it scales with volume the same way the subscription price does.
explanation.volume-doubling: Applicable. Usage-based pricing means the effective monthly cost next year is not the number in this quote — it's the number times roughly two, which changes the comparison against hiring meaningfully.
explanation.correction-rate: Applicable. This is the number that determines how much review labor the tool actually generates — it's the load-bearing figure the 95% headline was hiding.
explanation.vendor-founded-recently: Not applicable to the cost comparison. Company age says nothing about what this tool will actually cost Halsted to run — it's the kind of detail that feels like due diligence but doesn't move the number.
explanation.demo-looked-good: Not applicable, and specifically the trap this lesson is about — a demo run on the vendor's own clean sample documents tells you nothing about performance on Halsted's actual mixed, scanned, non-standard submissions.
explanation.retest-owner: Applicable. An unscoped, unassigned maintenance task is a cost exactly as real as a budgeted one — it just lands as someone's unplanned time instead of a line item, which is precisely the gap the previous lesson's weekend-build example fell into.

contentSections.synthesis: The four facts that hold up are all things that turn a subscription price into an actual operating cost: labor that scales with volume, pricing that scales with volume, the correction rate that determines how much labor, and an unassigned maintenance task that will land on somebody regardless of whether it's budgeted. The two that don't hold up are about the vendor's story, not Halsted's bill.

contentSections.body: A vendor's sticker price is the start of a total-cost conversation, not the end of it. Review labor, exception handling, volume-scaling, and maintenance are usually most of what a tool actually costs, and none of them are on the quote.

title: Lock-in and what leaving would cost
description: Lock-in has specific, nameable sources — proprietary output formats, workflows only expressible in one vendor's tool, and configuration only one person understands — and the question to ask is before signing, not after.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the specific sources that create lock-in to a vendor
Ask the leaving-cost question before signing rather than after

contentSections.body: Halsted's previous claims-system migration took fourteen months, most of it spent on one problem: the old vendor stored adjuster notes in a proprietary field format nobody could cleanly export, so every note had to be manually re-copied into the new system. The team now evaluating the claims-extraction vendor is about to sign a contract without asking the equivalent question about this vendor's output format.

Lock-in isn't a vague feeling about a vendor being hard to leave — it comes from specific, nameable sources, and each one is a question you can ask before signing.

**Proprietary output format.** If extracted data is stored in the vendor's own schema rather than something standard and exportable, leaving means a re-mapping project, not a data export — this is exactly what cost Halsted fourteen months last time.

**A workflow only expressible in that vendor's tool.** If the sequence of steps — extract, route, flag for review — is built using the vendor's proprietary workflow builder, that logic doesn't travel with you; it has to be rebuilt from scratch in whatever replaces it.

**Trained or tuned assets tied to the platform.** Any model fine-tuning, prompt library, or custom classification rules built inside the vendor's platform typically don't export either — the vendor did the training, on the vendor's infrastructure, in a form only that platform can run.

**Institutional knowledge.** The softest and most common source: only one person at Halsted actually understands how the tool is configured, and that knowledge leaves when they do, vendor contract or not.

The question that surfaces all four is one sentence, asked at the negotiating table, not after the invoice arrives: "if we left in a year, what exactly would we take with us, and in what format?"

contentSections.scenario: The claims-extraction vendor's contract, section on data: "Extracted claim data is stored within the Client's account on the Vendor Platform and is accessible via the Platform dashboard and standard export functions." A second clause, in the technical appendix: "Field-mapping rules and extraction templates configured by the Client are proprietary Platform assets and are retained by Vendor upon termination."
contentSections.question: Which clause is doing the actual lock-in work here, and what specifically would Halsted lose on leaving?

options.label: The second clause — the field-mapping rules and extraction templates Halsted configures over time don't leave with them, so a new vendor means rebuilding that configuration from zero
The first clause — storing data 'within the Client's account' means Halsted doesn't actually own it
Neither — standard export functions mean this contract carries no real lock-in risk

feedback.second-clause: Correct. The first clause sounds reassuring — data is exportable — but the second one is where the actual dependency lives: the configuration Halsted builds over months of tuning field mappings and exception rules doesn't travel, so leaving means starting that tuning process over with the next vendor, which is a real, underestimated cost even when the raw data itself exports cleanly.
feedback.first-clause: The first clause is actually the more favorable one here — 'accessible via standard export functions' is a genuinely good sign for the raw data. The risk is specifically in what the export doesn't include.
feedback.no-lock-in: Standard export of the raw data is real, but it isn't the whole picture — the field-mapping rules and extraction templates are exactly the kind of institutional configuration work that's expensive to rebuild, and the contract explicitly says those don't come with you.

contentSections.mechanism: Lock-in often hides behind a genuinely true, reassuring clause about data portability, while the actual dependency sits in a second clause about configuration, workflow logic, or tuned assets that the first clause doesn't cover. Reading only as far as "yes, we can export our data" misses exactly the part worth negotiating.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order that gets the leaving-cost question answered before Halsted signs, not after they're already dependent on the vendor.
steps: List what Halsted would need to reconstruct if this vendor disappeared tomorrow: data, workflow logic, and tuned configuration, separately
Ask the vendor directly, in writing, what format each of those three exports in on termination
Ask who at Halsted currently understands, or will understand, the configuration well enough to explain it to a replacement vendor
Negotiate an export or portability clause for whichever of the three the vendor's default terms don't cover
Put the answer in the actual contract, not in an email the vendor forgets by renewal time
contentSections.explanation: You can't ask a useful question about exit cost until you've separated data, workflow logic, and configuration, because vendors answer the data part readily and the other two rarely come up unprompted — which is exactly the gap in Halsted's contract in this lesson. Asking who understands the configuration internally matters because institutional knowledge doesn't show up in any vendor's contract at all. Negotiating a fix only makes sense once you know which of the three is actually exposed. And the last step is the one that gets skipped under signing pressure: a verbal or emailed assurance from a sales contact doesn't survive that person changing roles, but contract language does.

contentSections.body: Lock-in comes from specific sources — output format, workflow logic, tuned assets, institutional knowledge — and each is a question worth asking, in writing, before signing. "Can we export our data" is necessary and not sufficient.

title: Evaluating a vendor in a week
description: A compressed evaluation timeline tempts every shortcut this module argues against — trusting the demo, skipping your own test documents, leaving cost and exit questions for later. A one-week evaluation that's still honest needs a fixed, minimal checklist.

learningObjectives.text: Run a compressed, honest vendor evaluation within a tight timeframe using a fixed test set and specific questions
Identify which shortcuts a tight timeline tempts, and which of them are actually safe to take

contentSections.body: Halsted's system-renewal deadline means the claims-extraction vendor decision has to be made in five working days, not the unhurried quarter the last full evaluation took. The temptation, with a deadline like that, is to let the vendor's live demo stand in for testing, and to sign on the vendor's own accuracy figure rather than Halsted's.

A one-week evaluation can still be honest, but only if it's built around a fixed, minimal checklist rather than however much time is left after the vendor's sales calls.

**Day 1–2: build your own test set.** Pull 15–20 of Halsted's own real, redacted claim documents, deliberately including the hardest ones — a scanned form, an unusual broker template, a claim with an ambiguous amount field. This is non-negotiable even under time pressure, because a vendor's demo is run on the vendor's own cleanest documents by definition.

**Day 2–3: run the tool against it.** Not a guided demo — your documents, your account, results you can actually inspect.

**Day 3–4: get the total-cost and lock-in questions answered in writing** — review-labor expectations, usage-based pricing at your real projected volume, and what specifically exports on termination.

**Day 5: decide, and write down the conditions that would change the decision.** A rushed decision is still better than a bad one, and naming the conditions that would flip it is what stops the deadline from quietly becoming "we didn't have time to check."

contentSections.title: What the deadline tempts you to skip
The vendor offers to run the test for you
contentSections.opening: Day 2 of five. The vendor, sensing the deadline, offers: "send us your documents and we'll run the extraction and send back the results by tomorrow morning — saves you the setup time."

offer.situation: You need to decide how to respond before end of day.
offer.question: What's the right move?

choices.label: Accept — it saves a day you don't have, and the documents are the same either way
choices.consequence: The documents may be the same, but who runs the test isn't a detail — a vendor running its own test on its own account, with its own defaults and its own thresholds tuned in its favor, is not the same evidence as Halsted running it themselves and seeing exactly what a reviewer would see day to day.

choices.label: Decline, and ask for direct trial access to run it yourself, even if that costs half a day of setup
choices.consequence: Setting up your own access costs time on a tight week, but it's the difference between a result you can trust and a result the vendor selected the framing for — and it's exactly the kind of shortcut worth refusing even under deadline pressure.

choices.label: Let the vendor run half the documents and run the other half yourself, to save time
choices.consequence: This looks like a reasonable compromise, but it doesn't actually solve the problem — the vendor still controls the conditions on their half, and a client evaluating a mixed result has no clean way to tell which half's numbers to trust for the final decision.

setup.situation: You get trial access and run all 18 of your own documents yourself, on day 2–3 as planned. Four of the hardest ones — the scanned form and the ambiguous-amount claim — come back wrong or flagged low-confidence.
setup.question: How do you use that result with two days left?

choices.label: Report the real number — 14 of 18 correct, with the four failures named specifically — and use the remaining time on cost and exit questions
choices.consequence: This is what the timeline was built to protect: a real result, even an imperfect one, used to inform the actual decision instead of a vendor-run number nobody stress-tested.

choices.label: Quietly drop the four hardest documents from the count and report the remaining 14 as "perfect on Halsted's document set"
choices.consequence: This produces a number that looks better and means nothing — it's the same move as reporting only the accepted side of a screening process. The four dropped documents are exactly the ones a reviewer will actually encounter in production.

outsourced.summary: The result you get back is the vendor's chosen framing of the vendor's own test, on a deadline too tight to double-check it. If the number is wrong in the vendor's favor, there's no time left in the week to find out.
outsourced.lesson: A deadline is a reason to test efficiently, not a reason to let the vendor test itself — those are different things that feel similar under time pressure.

diluted.summary: The final number is a blend of a result you can trust and one you can't, with no way to separate them — which means the decision is only as reliable as its worse half, while looking as reliable as its better half.
diluted.lesson: A compromise that mixes trustworthy and untrustworthy evidence into one number is often worse than picking one method cleanly, because the mixed number hides which part to distrust.

misleading.summary: Halsted signs believing the tool is "perfect" on its own documents. The first month in production, the same four failure types show up at volume, and now it's a production incident instead of a known, planned-for limitation.
misleading.lesson: A number built by dropping the hard cases isn't a faster version of the honest number — it's a different, false claim, and the gap between them lands during production instead of during evaluation.

honest.summary: Halsted signs knowing exactly which four situations need extra reviewer attention from day one, with a contract that answers the cost and exit questions this module raised, all inside the five-day deadline.
honest.lesson: A tight timeline doesn't have to mean a dishonest evaluation — it means being deliberate about which four days go to your own test and which one goes to the questions that don't need a test at all.

contentSections.body: A one-week evaluation is still an evaluation. Build your own hard test set even under deadline pressure, run it yourself rather than letting the vendor run it, and spend the time you save on cost and exit questions instead of skipping them.

title: Practice — Shortlist Tools for Seven Briefs with a Stated Criterion
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a brief and one stated criterion — cost, exit, support, or fit — apply this module's questions to shortlist or evaluate a tool.

learningObjectives.text: Apply the module's tool-category and total-cost distinctions to new briefs
Shortlist or reject a tool option using a single stated evaluation criterion

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Run a Structured Tool Evaluation Against Real Criteria
description: Pick a real or realistic automation need, evaluate at least one candidate tool against your own test set and this module's total-cost and lock-in criteria, and write a recommendation that states what would change it.

learningObjectives.text: Run a structured tool evaluation against a self-built test set and explicit cost and lock-in criteria
Produce a scored recommendation that states the conditions that would change it

contentSections.body: Every tool decision in this module got more defensible the moment it was tested against real documents and real cost questions instead of a vendor's pitch. That's the lab: pick one automation need — from your own work, a client's, or a plausible one you can specify concretely — and run it through this module's whole evaluation: category, total cost, lock-in, and a scored recommendation.

contentSections.title: Your structured tool evaluation
contentSections.brief: Pick one specific automation need — real or a concretely specified plausible one — where you or a client is deciding between tool options. You're going to name which category actually addresses it, evaluate at least one real candidate against your own test material, and end with a scored comparison and a written recommendation.
contentSections.deliverable: A scored comparison: the need stated concretely, the category it belongs to, at least one candidate evaluated against your own test material, a total-cost and lock-in assessment, and a recommendation naming the conditions that would change it.

stages.title: Name the need and its category
stages.instructions: State the automation need concretely — not 'we need AI for X' but the actual task, its current manual cost, and its input variability. Using this module's four categories (existing software, orchestration, RPA, model), name which one actually addresses it, and check explicitly whether an existing, already-licensed tool could solve part or all of it.
stages.checkpoint: You have a concrete need statement and a category decision with a one-line reason, including an explicit note on whether existing software was checked.

stages.title: Build a test set and evaluate at least one candidate
stages.instructions: Assemble 8-12 real or realistic test examples, including at least two deliberately hard ones. Evaluate at least one candidate tool against them — a real vendor, an open-source option, or a specified build approach — and log results honestly, the way the capability-testing lab from the previous phase did.
stages.checkpoint: You have a logged result for every test example, with hard cases flagged, not blended into an average.

stages.title: Assess total cost and lock-in
stages.instructions: For your leading candidate, name the review-labor, exception-handling, and volume-scaling costs beyond any sticker price, and name the specific lock-in sources (output format, workflow logic, tuned assets, institutional knowledge) and what leaving would actually cost.
stages.checkpoint: You have a total-cost estimate beyond the sticker price, and a lock-in assessment naming at least one specific exit cost.

stages.title: Write the scored recommendation
stages.instructions: Write the recommendation the way it would actually go to a decision-maker: the candidate, the score against your criteria, and — explicitly — the conditions under which you'd recommend differently (a cost threshold, a volume level, a data-format change).
stages.checkpoint: Your recommendation names at least one concrete condition that would change it, not just a confidence statement.

rubric.criterion: The need is stated concretely, not as a category or vendor name
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the situation could understand the actual task, its current manual cost, and its input variability.

rubric.criterion: Existing software was explicitly checked before any new tool
rubric.meets: The write-up states what was checked and what was found, even if the answer was 'no existing capability covers this.'

rubric.criterion: Test results are logged honestly, hard cases included
rubric.meets: Every test example has a recorded outcome, and difficult cases are visible as their own line, not averaged away.

rubric.criterion: Total cost goes beyond the sticker price
rubric.meets: Review labor, exception handling, and volume-scaling are each addressed, even briefly, with a real estimate.

rubric.criterion: Lock-in is assessed by specific source, not by vague impression
rubric.meets: At least one of output format, workflow logic, tuned assets, or institutional knowledge is named with what leaving would actually cost.

rubric.criterion: The recommendation states what would change it
rubric.meets: At least one concrete condition (a number, a format, a volume level) is named that would flip the recommendation.

contentSections.body: A recommendation tested against your own documents and your own cost questions is worth more than any vendor's pitch deck — and it's the only version of the recommendation you're entitled to put your name on.

title: Checkpoint — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's tool-selection distinctions, and earlier modules' capability and oversight distinctions, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Choosing Tools You Can Defend

questions.from: This module — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
questions.prompt: Halsted's claims system turns out to already have an unused email-ingestion feature. What's the right order to check tool categories in?

options.label: Whichever category is newest, since that's usually most capable
Existing software first, then orchestration or RPA to connect what exists, then a model only for the genuinely language-understanding piece
A model API first, since it's the most flexible option

questions.explanation: The existing claims system's unused ingestion module was the cheapest fix with no new vendor risk — checking it first is what the whole first lesson turns on.

questions.from: This module — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
questions.prompt: Why did the analyst's free weekend-build script end up costing Halsted three weeks of silent wrong extractions?

options.label: Python was the wrong tool for the job
The plan had no named owner and no drift detection for when a broker's template changed
The script was too slow to keep up with claim volume

questions.explanation: The plan was scoped only to the current templates, with nobody assigned to notice or fix a template change — an unassigned maintenance task is a cost exactly as real as a budgeted one, it just lands unpredictably.

questions.from: This module — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
questions.prompt: A vendor quotes $600/month and claims 95% accuracy. What did Halsted's own testing reveal that the quote didn't?

options.label: The tool was actually free to use
24% of Halsted's real, varied claim documents needed a human correction — the review labor and volume-scaling costs the quote never mentioned
The vendor's accuracy figure was fabricated

questions.explanation: The 95% figure was measured on the vendor's own benchmark; Halsted's actual mixed broker templates produced a 24% correction rate, which is the number that actually determines review-labor cost.

questions.from: This module — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
questions.prompt: A vendor contract says extracted data exports in a standard format, but field-mapping rules and extraction templates are "proprietary Platform assets retained by Vendor upon termination." What does this actually mean for Halsted?

options.label: Nothing — since the raw data exports, there's no real lock-in
The configuration work Halsted builds up over time doesn't travel, so leaving means rebuilding that tuning from zero with a new vendor
Halsted legally owns none of its own claims data

questions.explanation: The reassuring data-export clause hides the actual dependency in a second clause — months of field-mapping and exception-rule tuning don't come with you, which is real, underestimated exit cost.

questions.from: Previous module — Naming the Risk Before You're Paid
questions.prompt: Per the previous module, when should the failure modes of a proposed automation be named to a client?

options.label: After the engagement is signed, once real failures start appearing
In the proposal, while the client can still say no
Only if the client specifically asks about risk

questions.explanation: Naming what can go wrong, how badly, and who bears it belongs in the proposal itself, while the client still has a real choice — not discovered together after signing.

questions.from: Previous module — Naming the Risk Before You're Paid

options.label: Silent failures are always more frequent
A loud failure gets caught and fixed quickly; a silent one can run for a long time doing damage nobody's positioned to notice
Loud failures are more expensive to fix technically

questions.explanation: Two designs with the same error rate carry different risk depending on whether the errors announce themselves — the whole reason silent failure gets its own category in the risk-framing module.

questions.from: Previous module — Naming the Risk Before You're Paid
questions.prompt: What does the previous module say about regulated processes specifically?

options.label: Regulated processes should generally be avoided as clients entirely
There are specific questions worth asking before scoping a regulated process, because the risk profile is different from an unregulated one
Regulation doesn't meaningfully change how an automation should be scoped

questions.from: Previous module — Naming the Risk Before You're Paid

options.label: Never — a consultant should always find a way to deliver what's asked
When the honest risk assessment doesn't support what's being asked for, and it can be done professionally rather than dramatically
Only when the client can't pay
